Grudgingly
GRUJ-ing-lee
adv. (unwillingly; with reluctance; literally, out of grief)
From grudge, Old French grouchier, to murmur. The Greek behind the Authorized Version's word is literally of grief — giving out of sorrow at the giving. It occurs once.

Biblical Definition

Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver. Paul is arranging the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem, and the whole of 2 Corinthians 9 is about how the money is to be given rather than how much. Three things are excluded: grief at the giving, compulsion from outside, and the sparing calculation that hedges — he which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully. What is required is purpose in the heart and cheerfulness in the act, and the Greek word for cheerful is the one English gets hilarious from. The promise attached is not a promise of wealth but of sufficiency for further giving: God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work. The chapter ends where all Christian giving has to end, with the gift no one could match or repay: Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): unwillingly; with reluctance; in Scripture, the manner of giving which God does not accept, set against the cheerful giver he loves.

expand to see more

GRUDGINGLY, adv. Unwillingly; with reluctance; with discontent.

GRUDGE, v.i. To be discontented at another's enjoyments or advantages; to envy; to be unwilling to give.

CHEERFUL, a. Lively; animated; having good spirits; full of life and gladness.

LIBERALITY, n. Munificence; bounty; a particular act of generosity; a gift.

STEWARDSHIP, n. The office of a steward; the management of another's property.

Key Scripture

2Co 9:7 — "Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."

2Co 9:6 — "But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully."

2Co 9:8 — "And God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work:"

2Co 9:15 — "Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift."

Modern Corruption

Giving is either extracted by pressure and guilt or promised back with interest as an investment; Paul forbids compulsion, forbids grief in the giving, and promises sufficiency for further good works rather than gain.

expand to see more

Two opposite abuses of this chapter are common in the modern church. The first is the pressure appeal — the emotional squeeze, the public pledge card, the implication that a reluctant giver is not a real Christian. Paul excludes it in four words: not grudgingly, or of necessity. He would not even take the Corinthians' collection as a matter of commandment, saying he spoke not by commandment but to prove the sincerity of their love. The second abuse is the prosperity appeal, which reads sow bountifully and reap bountifully as an investment contract with God. The reaping Paul names in the next verse is all sufficiency in all things so that you may abound to every good work — enough, so that you can give again.

The chapter's foundation is not a technique of fundraising but a fact. He that ministereth seed to the sower both minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits of your righteousness. The giver is giving what he was given, and the increase is God's doing. That is why cheerfulness is the fitting manner: a man who understands that he is passing on a gift has nothing to grieve over in the passing. Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift — the sentence the whole appeal rests on and ends with.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek lupe (G3077), grief or sorrow, in the phrase rendered grudgingly; hilaros (G2431), cheerful; anagke (G318), necessity or compulsion.

expand to see more

Greek lupe (G3077) — grief, sorrow, pain; literally, not of grief — rendered grudgingly.

Greek hilaros (G2431) — cheerful, joyous, propitious; God loveth a cheerful giver.

Greek anagke (G318) — necessity, constraint; nor of necessity.

Greek proaireomai (G4255) — to purpose beforehand, to choose; as he purposeth in his heart.

Greek anekdiegetos (G411) — unspeakable, indescribable; his unspeakable gift.

Usage

"“not grudgingly, or of necessity” — the single occurrence."

"“for God loveth a cheerful giver” — the manner required."

"“Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift” — where the appeal ends."
